chapter: Boston roadhouses and the Army band
title: Learn to read, white musicians in Boston, and Caruso directing at a Reading roadhouse
summary: He says Boston jobs were all colored until the 1918 war, and describes a 1912 Sunday job where Caruso directed overtures and tipped $200 to the band.

story.theme_name: Drafted: musicians in the military and the war years
story.community_name: Drafted: service bands, USO shows and the war years

blocks.x: Oh, yeah, when I came to New York I used to tell everybody learn how to read. If you can't read, you can't read because up until the war in 1918 the white musicians weren't known in Boston, everything was colored. Colored musicians had all the jobs and then after the world war there was a -- the white musicians swept us away, but in 1912 I got a job out in Reading, Massachusetts, out at a road house and every Sunday when Enrico Caruso would come to Boston at the opera house, he'd come down there and Sunday afternoon at 2 o'clock and he'd stand up there and direct -- we'd play all the overtures. "Merry Wives of Windsor" and all those overtures, he would direct. He wouldn't sing, but he would direct.
And then we'd drink champagne and then when he'd get ready to go he'd give us $200 and divide it amongst the band. And 13, 14, Leroy Johnson was playing down to roadhouse
